problem: How to choose the objective function for the adversarial optimization when many formulations are possible.
did: They systematically compared seven objective functions crossed with three box-constraint encodings on MNIST and CIFAR, then adopted the best (f6, logit-based).
stated_reason: Empirically identifying the most effective formulation; there is a factor of three difference between best and worst, and cross entropy, the literature's favorite, performed worst.
quote: For each possible objective function $f(\cdot)$ and method to enforce the box constraint, we evaluate the quality of the adversarial examples found.
title: Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks

problem: Which evaluation of a defense is needed beyond running a stronger direct attack on the distilled network.
did: They added a transferability test using high-confidence adversarial examples (varying kappa) from an undefended model to the distilled model as a second break.
stated_reason: Any defense must break transferability, otherwise attackers could attack an easy model and transfer, and this works even if gradients are blocked.
quote: Even though defensive distillation is not robust to our stronger attacks, we demonstrate a second break of distillation by transferring attacks from a standard model to a defensively distilled model.
title: Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks

problem: How to define the target class for evaluating attack strength so results are not cherry-picked.
did: They ran best-case, average-case, and worst-case target selection in all evaluations, and sampled 100 targets on ImageNet.
stated_reason: Untargeted attacks are strictly less powerful and the paper focuses on the most accurate attacks; sampling on ImageNet is for efficiency.
quote: In all of our evaluations we perform all three types of attacks: best-case, average-case, and worst-case. Notice that if a classifier is only accurate $80\%$ of the time, then the best case attack will require a change of $0$ in $20\%$ of cases.
title: Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks

problem: How to ensure a fair baseline comparison against the prior distillation work and defense.
did: They reproduced the original model architectures, hyperparameters and training exactly, even though it yields lower CIFAR accuracy than state of the art, and did not add augmentation or dropout.
alternatives_named: training a state-of-the-art CIFAR model (95% accuracy)
stated_reason: To provide the most accurate comparison to the original work.
quote: However, in order to provide the most accurate comparison to the original work, we feel it is important to reproduce their model architectures.
title: Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks

problem: Whether to report exact runtimes when comparing attacks with unequal implementations.
did: They declined to report exact performance numbers and gave only coarse relative runtime statements.
stated_reason: Implementations differ in parallelization, so they believe an unfair comparison is worse than no comparison.
quote: We therefore refrain from giving exact performance numbers because we believe an unfair comparison is worse than no comparison.
title: Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks

problem: Why distillation appeared to defend against existing attacks and whether this reflects real robustness.
did: They investigated the failure of existing attacks and concluded that vanishing gradients (float rounding) made the attacks fragile, not the network robust, and verified with a temperature sweep using their own attack.
alternatives_named: interpreting low attack success as genuine robustness
stated_reason: Mean L2 distance showed no correlation with temperature, so higher temperature only makes existing attacks fail more often.
quote: This clearly demonstrates the fact that increasing the distillation temperature does not increase the robustness of the neural network, it only causes existing attacks to fail more often.
title: Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks

problem: Whether rounding continuous adversarial examples to valid images invalidates reported results.
did: They included discretization post-processing (rounding plus greedy lattice search) in all reported success rates.
alternatives_named: ignoring integrality constraints as prior work did
stated_reason: Their attacks make much smaller changes, so discretization effects cannot be ignored.
quote: We take care to always generate valid images; when reporting the success rate of our attacks, they always are for attacks that include the discretization post-processing.
title: Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks

problem: How to handle the L-infinity objective, where naive gradient descent oscillates.
did: They abandoned directly minimizing the L-infinity norm and replaced it with an iterative attack penalizing all terms exceeding a shrinking threshold tau.
stated_reason: The L-infinity term only penalizes the largest entry, so gradient descent oscillates between two suboptimal solutions.
quote: We resolve this issue using an iterative attack. We replace the $L_{2}$ term in the objective function with a penalty for any terms that exceed $\tau$ (initially $1$, decreasing in each iteration).
title: Towards Evaluating the Robustness of Neural Networks

problem: How to evaluate whether a detection defense is robust given varying attacker knowledge.
did: They evaluated each defense under three threat models (zero-knowledge, perfect-knowledge, limited-knowledge) using a strong attack, an adaptive white-box attack, and a transfer-based black-box attack.
alternatives_named: evaluating only with weak attacks like fast gradient sign and JSMA
evaluating only against an oblivious attacker
stated_reason: The zero-knowledge test is the weakest threat model so failing it implies failing the others; the black-box test is only interesting if zero-knowledge failed and white-box succeeded.
quote: In this step we generate adversarial examples with C&W’s attack and check whether the defense can detect this strong attack. This evaluation approach has the weakest threat model (the attacker is not even aware the defense is in place), so any defense should trivially be able to detect this attack.
title: Adversarial Examples Are Not Easily Detected: Bypassing Ten Detection Methods

problem: Which attack to use for generating adversarial examples when testing the defenses.
did: They used the C&W L2 targeted attack rather than FGS or JSMA used in the original defense papers.
stated_reason: These attacks are weaker than C&W's attack, and weak attacks give a biased view of defense robustness.
quote: Aside from C&W’s attack, the Fast Gradient Sign attack (Goodfellow et al., 2014) and JSMA (Papernot et al., 2016b) are two attacks used by some defenses for evaluation. These attacks are weaker than C&W’s attack and we do not use them for evaluation
title: Adversarial Examples Are Not Easily Detected: Bypassing Ten Detection Methods

problem: How to interpret the large detectable difference between natural and adversarial examples in PCA on MNIST.
did: They investigated the cause of the difference and found it was an artifact of MNIST border pixels, not an intrinsic property of adversarial examples, and checked CIFAR.
alternatives_named: concluding PCA is a powerful and effective detector
stated_reason: Large abnormalities in data require understanding their cause; the difference arises because border pixels are nearly always zero in natural MNIST images.
quote: At first glance, this might lead us to believe that PCA is a powerful and effective method for detecting adversarial examples. However, whenever there are large abnormalities in the data, one must be careful to understand their cause.
title: Adversarial Examples Are Not Easily Detected: Bypassing Ten Detection Methods

problem: Whether the failure of Bhagoji's dimensionality reduction defense to improve robustness is due to the network architecture rather than the defense.
did: They tested a second Bhagoji algorithm combining PCA projection with a convolutional network, holding architecture fixed so only dimensionality reduction varies.
alternatives_named: comparing only the fully-connected PCA model to a convolutional baseline
stated_reason: To show the result is not an artifact of fully-connected networks being less robust than convolutional ones.
quote: This allows us to perform an experiment where the network architecture is held fixed, and the only change is whether dimensionality reduction is used or not.
title: Adversarial Examples Are Not Easily Detected: Bypassing Ten Detection Methods

problem: What to do when the generic combined-function attack on the dropout randomization defense failed.
did: They diagnosed that the function U is computed on probabilities F not logits Z, abandoned the single combined function, and instead changed the loss to sum over several sampled deterministic networks.
alternatives_named: constructing a single function G to optimize over
stated_reason: Because U is computed from F rather than Z, there is no good constant c, so gradient descent performs poorly.
quote: Therefore, for this defense, we abandon the approach of constructing a single function to optimize over and instead change the loss function $\ell$ used by the attack.
title: Adversarial Examples Are Not Easily Detected: Bypassing Ten Detection Methods

problem: Whether a failed first attack attempt shows a defense is robust.
did: They treated the initial 60% detection as an attack-design failure and investigated why, rather than accepting the defense as effective.
alternatives_named: accepting that the defense detects adversarial examples
stated_reason: The choice of loss function is critical; the obvious loss often makes a defense appear more robust than it is.
quote: We discover that the specific loss function chosen is critical to effectively defeating the defense: choosing the immediately obvious loss function often results in the defense appearing significantly more robust than it actually is.
title: Adversarial Examples Are Not Easily Detected: Bypassing Ten Detection Methods

problem: How to characterize the dropout defense's limited-knowledge result, where the transfer attack needs only 15% more distortion.
did: They framed the result as a success of the defense under the white-box model and called it the only defense not completely broken.
alternatives_named: calling it a failure of the defense under the black-box threat model
stated_reason: It made adaptive white-box attacks nearly as hard as black-box attacks.
quote: While this $15\%$ increase may seem like a failure of this defense under the black-box threat model, we see this instead as a success of defense under the white-box threat model.
title: Adversarial Examples Are Not Easily Detected: Bypassing Ten Detection Methods

problem: Which datasets to use for evaluating the defenses.
did: They evaluated on both MNIST and CIFAR-10 and found that MNIST results do not carry over to CIFAR.
stated_reason: Defenses evaluated only on MNIST were typically useless or weaker on CIFAR, so MNIST alone is not sufficient.
quote: Future schemes need to be evaluated on multiple data sets — evaluating their security solely on MNIST is not sufficient.
title: Adversarial Examples Are Not Easily Detected: Bypassing Ten Detection Methods

problem: How to make the limited-knowledge evaluation of Grosse's defense a fair test of transfer.
did: They split the training set in half, giving the attacker one half with white-box access to model R1 and testing transfer to the defender's model R2 trained on the other half.
alternatives_named: training one model on the complete training set
stated_reason: The attacker should not have the exact model parameters or training data of the secured model.
quote: Instead of training one model on the complete training set, we split the training set in half. We assume the first half is known to the attacker and the second half is used by the defender to train their network.
title: Adversarial Examples Are Not Easily Detected: Bypassing Ten Detection Methods

problem: How to measure unintended memorization when raw log-perplexity values depend heavily on model, application, and dataset.
did: They inserted random canaries and measured a relative exposure metric comparing the canary's perplexity to that of equivalent non-inserted random sequences.
alternatives_named: directly reporting the log-perplexity of the training data
stated_reason: Raw log-perplexity is high or low depending on the specific model, application, or dataset, so it is ill suited as a direct measure of memorization.
quote: Naively, we might try to measure a model’s unintended memorization of training data by directly reporting the log-perplexity of that data. However, whether the log-perplexity value is high or low depends heavily on the specific model, application, or dataset
title: The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks

problem: How to efficiently estimate exposure when the inserted canary has rank near 1 and random sampling rarely finds lower-perplexity candidates.
did: They modeled the canary perplexity distribution with a skew-normal and extrapolated from it, checking the fit with a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test.
stated_reason: Sampling is inefficient when only very few alternate canaries have lower perplexity, since sampling distribution extremes is difficult.
quote: However, this sampling method is inefficient if only very few alternate canaries have lower entropy than $s[r]$, in which case $|S|$ may have to be large to obtain an accurate estimate.
title: The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks

problem: Whether the exposure metric actually corresponds to real extractability of memorized sequences.
did: They built a shortest-path extraction algorithm and tested whether high exposure implies extraction across models trained to the same test accuracy, looking for false positives.
stated_reason: The underlying hypothesis is that exposure is a useful measure for judging when canaries have been memorized, so they check there are not many false positives.
quote: We now validate that when the exposure of a phrase is high, we can extract the phrase from the model (i.e., there are not many false positives, where exposure is high but we can’t extract it).
title: The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks

problem: Whether memorization detected with artificially inserted canaries is an artifact of the insertion.
did: They ran the extraction analysis on the Enron email dataset, which contains naturally occurring secrets such as SSNs and credit card numbers.
alternatives_named: experiments on data with artificially inserted canaries
stated_reason: It is possible, though unlikely, that memorization is detected only because canaries were artificially inserted.
quote: It is possible (although unlikely) that we detect memorization only because we have inserted our canaries artificially. To confirm this is not the case, we study a dataset that has many naturally-occurring secrets already in the training data.
title: The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks

problem: Whether unintended memorization is merely a consequence of overtraining, which standard regularization would fix.
did: They tested weight decay, dropout, and quantization, using a 5% PTB subset that overtrains so the regularizers could be assessed, and found none prevent memorization.
stated_reason: It might be reasonable to assume memorization stems from overtraining, so they test whether regularizers that prevent overtraining also prevent it.
quote: In order to directly measure the effect of weight decay on a model that does overtrain, we take the first $5\%$ of the PTB dataset and train our language model there.
title: The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks

problem: How to compare memorization across training strategies when models differ in final accuracy.
did: They controlled for final test accuracy by taking earlier checkpoints from better-performing models before comparing canary exposure.
stated_reason: Not all optimizers converge to the same final test accuracy, so differences in exposure could be confounded with accuracy.
quote: However, when we control for the final test accuracy by taking a checkpoint from an earlier epoch from those models that perform better, we found no statistically significant difference in the exposure of the canary
title: The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks

problem: Whether to continue pursuing automatic sanitization of training data via disagreement between two models as a defense.
did: They dropped the approach after finding it missed secrets and was unsound, and judged sanitization not an effective defense on its own.
stated_reason: The approach missed some secrets and is unsound if the same secret is inserted twice; black-listing is never complete in security.
quote: Unfortunately, this style of approach missed some secrets (and is unsound if the same secret is inserted twice).
title: The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks

problem: How to interpret exposure values near zero for DP models trained with very large, theoretically meaningless epsilon.
did: They interpreted the negligible measured exposure as evidence that the analytic epsilon bound is loose, citing related work on the gap between empirical and theoretical privacy loss.
stated_reason: Related studies found orders-of-magnitude gaps between measured privacy loss and the upper-bound epsilon, and improved proofs tighten guarantees without changing training.
quote: Even with a vanishingly-small amount of noise, and values of $\varepsilon$ that offer no meaningful theoretical guarantees, the measured exposure is negligible.
title: The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks

problem: How strongly to claim the practical meaning of extraction time on Enron data.
did: They cautioned that the local extraction time of a few hours should not be taken as the cost of a real attack.
stated_reason: The local attack batches queries and does not include remote querying in the run-time computation.
quote: Note that it would be unfair to draw from this that an actual attack would only take a few hours: this local attack can batch queries to the model and does not include any remote querying in the run-time computation.
title: The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks

problem: How to decide which attacks a defense evaluation must include to show real robustness rather than robustness to known attacks only.
did: Required that evaluators actively attempt to evade the specific defense with adaptive attacks after fully specifying it, rather than only testing against prior fixed attacks.
alternatives_named: evaluating only against previous or state-of-the-art attacks not targeting the specific defense
stated_reason: A defense only matters if it withstands future attacks; defeating a fixed attack is easy to achieve by subtly breaking that attack (like rot-14 vs rot-13), and non-adaptive attacks are already solved.
quote: The first, and by far most important, component of a defense evaluation is to attempt to evade the specific defense. After the defense has been defined, ask: what attack could possibly defeat this defense?
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

problem: Which attack strength and type to use when evaluating a defense's robustness, given that weak attacks can be defeated by gradient masking.
did: Recommended against relying on Fast Gradient Sign alone, and instead advised iterative attacks with 1000+ iterations.
stated_reason: FGS was never intended as a strong attack and weak adversarial training can defeat it via gradient masking; no reasonable threat model lets an attacker run 100 iterations but not 1000.
quote: There is no reasonable threat model under which an attacker can compute 10 (or 100) iterations of gradient descent, but not 1000. Because the threat model must not constrain the approach an attacker takes, it is always worth evaluating against a strong attack with many iterations of gradient descent.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

problem: How to detect whether a defense is causing gradient masking that fools gradient-based attacks.
did: Recommended also running gradient-free attacks (ZOO, SPSA, NES, decision-only) to check for gradient masking.
stated_reason: To ensure the model is not causing various forms of gradient masking.
quote: Apply gradient-free attacks. To ensure that the model is not causing various forms of gradient masking, it is worth attempting gradient-free attacks. There are several such proposals. I would recommend these four.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

problem: How to confirm that the attack suite is not missing obvious adversarial examples.
did: Recommended brute-force random search attacks as a sanity check, with a few hundred thousand random samples on about a hundred instances.
stated_reason: Random sampling confirms nothing obvious is missed, and if it finds adversarial examples other methods missed, then the other attacks can be improved.
quote: If brute-force random sampling identifies adversarial examples that other methods haven't found, this indicates that other attacks can be improved.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

problem: Whether to accept an iterative attack's results when they look worse than a simpler single-step attack.
did: Advised treating an iterative attack that underperforms a single-step attack as likely incorrect, and diagnosing it with plots of success rate and loss vs. iterations.
alternatives_named: accepting the weaker iterative attack results at face value
stated_reason: Iterative attacks are strictly more powerful than single-step attacks, so underperformance suggests the attack is flawed or the model is obfuscating gradients.
quote: Iterative attacks are strictly more powerful than single-step attacks, and so their results should be strictly superior. If an iterative attack performs worse than a single-step attack, this often indicates that the iterative attack is not correct.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

problem: Whether to accept an attack evaluation as sound when white-box attacks do worse than black-box attacks.
did: Advised treating black-box attacks outperforming white-box attacks as a sign of gradient masking or a weak white-box attack, and investigating the instances where only black-box succeeds.
stated_reason: White-box attacks are a strict superset of black-box attacks, so they should perform strictly better.
quote: Because white-box attacks are a strict superset of black-box attacks, they should perform strictly better. Black-box attacks doing better often indicates that the defense is somehow masking gradient information.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

problem: How to decide whether an attack is correctly implemented using sanity checks on unbounded and increasing-distortion settings.
did: Advised verifying that attack success increases monotonically with distortion and that unbounded attacks reach 100% success, treating violations as evidence of a flawed attack.
stated_reason: More distortion makes attacks strictly stronger, and with unbounded distortion any attack should eventually succeed, so violations indicate incorrect application.
quote: Verify that unbounded attacks always succeed. With unbounded distortion, any attack should eventually reach 100% success, if only by switching the input to actually be part of the other class.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

problem: How to compare defenses when one performs better on weak attacks but worse on strong ones, and how to compare across different attack regimes.
did: Recommended judging defenses by the worst-case (strongest) attack and not comparing numbers from fixed-attack evaluations against adaptive-attack evaluations.
alternatives_named: comparing defenses on weaker attacks such as FGS
comparing fixed-attack numbers of a new defense to adaptive-attack numbers of prior defenses
stated_reason: Comparing across different attack strengths is unfair, like comparing MLP accuracy on MNIST to ResNet accuracy on CIFAR.
quote: If Defense A does better than Defense B on weaker attacks (e.g., FGS) but does worse against a stronger attack (e.g., PGD), then Defense B is the stronger defense.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

problem: How to determine whether a defense's apparent robustness stems from gradient masking rather than genuine robustness.
did: They recommend applying gradient-free and hard-label attacks as a test for gradient masking, expecting them to do worse than gradient-based attacks.
stated_reason: Gradient-free attacks should almost always do worse than gradient-based ones, so white-box attacks doing worse is strong evidence of gradient masking.
quote: The most important reason to apply gradient-free attacks is as a test for gradient masking (Tramèr et al., 2017; Athalye et al., 2018; Uesato et al., 2018). Gradient-free attacks should almost always do worse than gradient-based attacks (see §5.2).
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

problem: How to decide whether an iterative attack has run for enough iterations to be a valid evaluation.
did: They recommend doubling the number of iterations and checking whether attack success improves, plus plotting success versus iterations.
alternatives_named: choosing a fixed bounded number of iterations
stated_reason: Any fixed iteration count is hard to generalize, so doubling is a simple test that the selected number is probably sufficient.
quote: Because choosing any fixed bounded number of iterations can be difficult to generalize, one simple and useful method for determining if “enough” iterations have been performed is to try doubling the number of iterations and check if this improves on the adversarial examples generated.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

problem: Which adversary model a defense evaluation should target and how to treat non-adaptive attacks.
did: They insist evaluations focus on adaptive adversaries who know the defense, and reject zero-knowledge and non-adaptive evaluations as nearly useless.
stated_reason: Existing attacks and hyperparameters were tuned only against existing defenses and may fail on a new defense, e.g. through gradient masking.
quote: Just applying existing adversarial attacks with default hyperparameters is not sufficient, even if these attacks are state-of-the-art: all existing attacks and hyperparameters have been adapted to and tested only against existing defenses
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

problem: How to decide whether to trust a newly proposed attack that fails to break a defense.
did: They recommend validating any new attack by running it on models known or designed to be insecure and confirming it breaks them.
stated_reason: It is easy to design an attack that is never effective regardless of the model it attacks.
quote: Therefore, when designing a new attack, it is important to validate that it is indeed effective. This can be done by selecting alternate models that are either known to be insecure or are intentionally designed to be insecure, and verify that the new attack algorithm can effectively break these defenses.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

problem: How to aggregate attack results across multiple attacks when reporting and comparing defenses.
did: They recommend reporting per-example worst-case success (best attack per example) rather than averaging per attack and taking the best attack.
alternatives_named: min over attacks of mean over examples
comparing defenses on different attacks X and Y
stated_reason: Per-example reporting is strictly more useful and avoids unhelpful comparisons where defenses are compared on different attacks.
quote: This per-example reporting is strictly more useful than a per-attack reporting, and is therefore preferable. This is true despite the fact that in practice the results for the worst attack is often very close to the true per-example worst-case bounds.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

problem: How to interpret a failure of attacks against a randomized defense.
did: They recommend first fixing the randomness to one value and confirming the attack succeeds, then slowly re-enabling randomness to see success decrease.
alternatives_named: accepting failed attacks as evidence of robustness
stated_reason: If attacks fail even with randomness disabled, the attack is likely not working correctly and should be fixed.
quote: If the attacks fail even when the randomness is disabled in this way, it is likely that the attack is not working correctly and should be fixed. Once the attack succeeds with randomness completely disabled
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

problem: How strongly to present the evaluation checklist and how authoritative it should be.
did: They explicitly frame the checklist as neither necessary nor sufficient, a living document of common flaws, warning against blindly following it.
alternatives_named: presenting the list as a definitive protocol
stated_reason: Blindly following the checklist without thought will likely be counterproductive; each item must be considered in the context of the specific defense.
quote: We encourage readers to be extremely careful and not directly follow this list to perform an evaluation or decide if an evaluation that has been performed is sufficient.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

problem: Whether to accept a prior defense's originally claimed accuracy when comparing against prior work that was later broken.
did: They recommend reporting prior defenses' accuracy under the strongest known attacks rather than the originally claimed number.
stated_reason: If follow-up work reduced a claimed accuracy, the original result is wrong.
quote: If a defense claimed that its accuracy was $99\%$ but followup work reduced its accuracy to $80\%$, future work should report the accuracy at $80\%$, and not $99\%$. The original result is wrong.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

problem: Which target model to attack so that extraction research can be done without causing real-world privacy harm and without the attacker unintentionally exploiting knowledge of the training data.
did: The authors chose GPT-2 as the attack target because its model and data are public but the dataset was never released.
alternatives_named: attacking models trained on private or sensitive data
stated_reason: Memorized data extracted is already public, and since the dataset was never released the attacks cannot unintentionally cheat using knowledge of the training set.
quote: First, from an ethical standpoint, the model and data are public, and so any memorized data that we extract is already public.
title: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models

problem: How to verify that candidate samples are truly memorized rather than just plausible or generic text.
did: The authors manually checked each of 1,800 samples via Google exact-match searches, then confirmed with the GPT-2 authors who ran fuzzy 3-gram matching and exact greps over the original training data.
stated_reason: The training data was public web text so searches work as the main tool; the 3-gram matching eliminates false negatives but has false positives, so it can only confirm memorization.
quote: We mark a sample as memorized if we can identify a non-trivial substring that returns an exact match on a page found by a Google search.
title: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models

problem: Perplexity-based membership inference yields many false positives (trivial or repeated text), so a better way to select memorized candidates is needed.
did: The authors compared GPT-2 likelihood against reference signals (smaller GPT-2 models, zlib entropy, lowercased text, sliding-window perplexity) to find samples with unexpectedly high likelihood.
alternatives_named: training a second model on disjoint data
stated_reason: Raw perplexity flags trivial memorization and repeated substrings, while a second model should also assign high likelihood to those, so a ratio filters them out.
quote: Our insight is that we can filter out these uninteresting (yet still high-likelihood samples) by comparing to a second LM.
title: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models

problem: The Internet-conditioned sampling strategy might overlap with GPT-2's training data and thereby unfairly inflate results.
did: The authors accepted the strategy as valid, collecting data differently from GPT-2 and arguing that overlap is rare and small in absolute terms since only 5-10 tokens are used.
alternatives_named: following Reddit links as GPT-2 did
stated_reason: Any overlap between the datasets is rare on average and only the first 5 to 10 tokens of each sample are used, so overlap is small in absolute terms.
quote: It is possible there is some intersection between these two datasets, effectively allowing this strategy to "cheat". We believe this does not considerably affect results.
title: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models

problem: How to study how many times a string must appear in training data to be memorized, without relying on synthetic canaries.
did: The authors used naturally occurring URLs repeated varying numbers of times in a single pastebin document as natural canaries, testing GPT-2 XL, Medium and Small with both a hard and an easier extraction approach.
alternatives_named: inserting synthetic canaries into the training data
stated_reason: Synthetic canaries are inserted artificially after dataset collection and may not be representative of natural data.
quote: The main limitation of this approach is that it is synthetic: canaries are inserted artificially after the dataset has been collected and may not be representative of natural data.
title: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models

problem: How strongly to claim the amount of memorization found, given that only simple prompts and a small inspected candidate set were used.
did: The authors stated that their 604 examples vastly under-estimate true memorization and are a loose lower bound.
stated_reason: Memorized content depends strongly on context, and there are likely prompts that would reveal much more memorized content, but the authors stuck to simple prompts and inspected only 1,800 candidates.
quote: The important lesson here is that our work vastly under-estimates the true amount of content that GPT-2 memorized.
title: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models

problem: Whether to pursue targeted extraction of specific users' data or indiscriminate extraction to study memorization.
did: The authors chose indiscriminate extraction rather than targeted attacks.
alternatives_named: targeted attacks on specific users or content
stated_reason: Their goal was to study the ability of LMs to memorize data generally, not to build an attack that real adversaries could operationalize against specific users.
quote: We do not aim to extract targeted pieces of training data, but rather indiscriminately extract training data.
title: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models

problem: How to measure whether poisoning-vulnerable datasets are actually still being downloaded by real clients, rather than by crawlers or other internet users.
did: They bought expired domains for each dataset, passively logged requests for 12 months, and identified dataset downloads using strict recall and precision criteria on source IPs.
alternatives_named: checking only 3 of the URLs instead of all 6 domains
stated_reason: The conditions are conservative and filter out web crawlers and mass scrapers, which would violate either the precision or recall constraint.
quote: These conditions are conservative, but ensure we filter out web crawlers and other mass internet scrapers because these are likely to crawl other URLs from this domain (violating the precision constraint) or not crawl the majority of the URLs from the dataset (violating the recall constraint).
title: Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical

problem: How to measure the speed at which Wikipedia vandalism is reverted, which determines the attacker's opportunity window.
did: They used a passive analysis of historical Wikipedia edits instead of injecting malicious edits and measuring reversion times.
alternatives_named: inject malicious edits and measure the distribution of reversion times
stated_reason: Injecting edits would be the most accurate methodology but they believe it would be unethical.
quote: Note that while the most accurate methodology would be to inject malicious edits and measure the distribution of reversion times, we believe this would be unethical. Instead, we take an entirely passive—albeit less accurate—approach as discussed in Section V-F.
title: Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical

problem: How to demonstrate that split-view poisoning is effective on large datasets without actually harming real users.
did: They did not poison any dataset; they returned 404s on the purchased domains and simulated the attack by locally replacing images and training an OpenCLIP model.
stated_reason: The local simulation shows the effect of an attack without any potential to cause harm to others.
quote: Then, we locally replace these images with poisoned samples to simulate the effect of an attack, without any potential to cause harm to others.
title: Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical

problem: How to determine whether the domain-purchase attack was already exploited in the wild, given the tradeoffs of image comparison methods.
did: They compared images with both perceptual (CLIP) similarity and cryptographic hashes and checked domain ownership changes, then investigated flagged domains individually before accepting them as evidence of an attack.
stated_reason: Cryptographic hashes have no false negatives but give false positives for benign changes, while perceptual hashes have fewer false positives but can be evaded by an adversary.
quote: Comparing images with cryptographic hashes has no false-negatives (i.e., any change is detected) but gives false-positives for “benign” changes, e.g., if a domain re-encodes or resizes its images.
title: Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical

problem: How strongly to claim the fraction of Wikipedia that could be poisoned, given estimation uncertainty and real-world limits like rate limiting and IP bans.
did: They used conservative lower bounds on the snapshot interval and reversion probability, reported 6.5% as a best-effort estimate, and acknowledged factors that could prevent reaching it.
alternatives_named: retrying edits on targeted articles to force repeated reversions
stated_reason: The analysis is pessimistic because it assumes a single attempt per article, and even the conservative estimate is orders of magnitude above the poisoning rates required in prior attacks.
quote: However, our analysis is also pessimistic since we assume we only try once to poison any given article. An adversary could attempt a more targeted attack where they retry edits on targeted articles
title: Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical

problem: How to interpret the systematic bias in the predicted Wikipedia snapshot times.
did: They attributed the negative bias to snapshots speeding up over time and corrected for it by introducing an adjustment variable a, optimized over a sweep.
alternatives_named: making edits exactly at the predicted time
stated_reason: Snapshots slightly speed up over time, so the next snapshot time is typically overestimated.
quote: We notice, however, that our extrapolation errors are biased towards negative. We find that this is because snapshots slightly speed up over time, so we typically overestimate the next snapshot time of an article.
title: Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical

problem: Which question about dataset poisoning to study, given the large existing literature on its impact, stealth and defenses.
did: They focused on the preliminary question of whether an adversary can actually get poisoned data into a web-scale dataset, rather than on poisoning impact, stealth or defenses.
stated_reason: There are already hundreds of papers dedicated to each of those other questions.
quote: Our paper does not address any of these questions as there are already hundreds of papers already dedicated to each. We focus on the preliminary question: is it actually possible for an adversary to actually poison a dataset?
title: Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical

problem: How to treat the reviewers' objection that the attack only works when standard integrity protections are absent.
did: They accepted the premise but argued the work is still valuable because every large dataset lacks these defenses and hashing degrades utility, so the vulnerability matters in practice.
alternatives_named: perceptual hashes instead of cryptographic hashes
stated_reason: Perfect defenses that are rarely applied are still worrying, and adding hashes significantly reduces dataset utility.
quote: Performing research on areas where perfect defenses exist, but are rarely used, is still valuable.
title: Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical

problem: Existing NLP attacks fail to elicit toxic output from aligned models, which could mean either that the models are robust or that the attacks are too weak.
did: They treated attack failure as ambiguous and tested attack strength directly using test cases with known, brute-force-constructed adversarial examples rather than concluding the models are robust.
alternatives_named: The aligned language models we attack are truly robust to adversarial examples
Current attacks are insufficiently powerful to evaluate the robustness of aligned models
stated_reason: Attack failure alone cannot distinguish robust defenses from weak attacks, so a framework with guaranteed-to-exist solutions is needed.
quote: To construct test cases, we first identify a set of adversarial examples via brute force. And once we have confirmed the existence of at least one adversarial example via brute force, we run our attack over the same search space
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: How to build test cases for attack strength when picking a toxic target ahead of time would make brute-force discovery of a prompt infeasible.
did: They dropped the requirement that the target be toxic and worked in reverse, sampling prefixes, enumerating contexts, and choosing the least-likely output token as the target.
stated_reason: If q were chosen ahead of time, it might be very hard to find, even via brute force, a prefix p such that Gen(p)=q.
quote: If we were to choose $q$ ahead of time, then it might be very hard to find—even via brute force—a prefix $p$ so that $\texttt{Gen}(p)=q$. So instead we drop the requirement that $q$ is toxic, and approach the problem from reverse.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: Which threat model to evaluate prior NLP attacks under: one where the attacker controls the tokens right before generation, or one matching chat-bot deployments with fixed special tokens after user input.
did: They evaluated attacks where the adversary controls only the user message and the [AGENT]: token is appended afterwards, rather than adopting the stronger threat model of Jones et al.
alternatives_named: attacker controls the entire prompt, Gen(X)
attacker controls the text immediately preceding the generation, Gen(P_pre||X)
stated_reason: The stronger threat model makes the attack much easier but does not match current chat-bot deployments.
quote: In both cases, the attacker controls the tokens right before the model’s generation, which makes an attack much easier (but not relevant for current chat bot deployments).
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: Where to generate brute-force test cases given the high cost of brute-force search, and whether results would transfer to harder aligned models.
did: They generated test cases using GPT-2 only, reasoning that failure on the easier model implies failure on harder aligned models.
alternatives_named: generating test cases on aligned models
stated_reason: Brute force is costly, and GPT-2 is easier to attack, so attack failures there are unlikely to be reversed on aligned models.
quote: We generate our test cases using GPT-2 only, due to the cost of running a brute force search. However, as GPT-2 is an easier model to attack, if attacks fail here, they are unlikely to succeed on the more difficult cases of aligned models.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: Whether the very low pass rates of prior attacks on the test set reflect a real weakness or just a too-restrictive token budget.
did: They gave the attacker more control by multiplying the number of attacker-controlled tokens up to 10x and checked whether the failure persisted.
stated_reason: Because the numbers were so low, they wanted to see whether extra attacker freedom would change the conclusion.
quote: Because the numbers here are so low, we then experimented with giving the attacker more control, with a multiplicative factor on the number of manipulated tokens.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: The simple substring-based isToxic metric could mislabel outputs as toxic, so it was unclear whether reported success rates were trustworthy.
did: They qualitatively inspected a subset of generations, found under ten cases where the metric was flawed, and kept the simple metric while acknowledging its limits.
stated_reason: Attacks currently have negligible success even under this loose definition, so a more careful definition is deferred until attacks achieve nontrivial success.
quote: Future work will need to carefully consider different toxicity definitions once attacks begin to have nontrivial attack success rates—for now, even with this loose definition, the current attacks in the literature fail to find successful adversarial sequences.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: How strongly to claim that text-only aligned models are vulnerable to adversarial inputs given that only multimodal attacks and attack-failure evidence exist.
did: They framed the claim as an explicit conjecture rather than a demonstrated result, supported by two lines of indirect evidence.
stated_reason: They cannot prove the claim, but believe the soft-embedding attacks and the known-to-exist-yet-unfound solutions provide strong evidence.
quote: While we cannot prove this claim (that’s why it’s a conjecture!) we believe our paper provides strong evidence for it: (1) language models are weak to soft-embedding attacks (e.g., multimodal attacks); and (2) current NLP attacks cannot find solutions that are known to exist.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: Directly optimizing the true toxicity objective over long generations is expensive, since backpropagation through many forward passes would be required.
did: They optimized a surrogate harmful-prefix objective, making the model begin its response with a malicious string, requiring only a single forward pass.
alternatives_named: directly optimizing isToxic(Gen(X)) over the full generated sequence
stated_reason: The surrogate is much easier to optimize, and once the model begins with harmful output it continues emitting harmful text without further adversarial control.
quote: instead of directly optimizing the true objective, i.e., checking that $\texttt{isToxic}(S)$ is true for a generated $S$, we optimize for the surrogate objective $S_{..j}=t$ for some malicious string $t$, with $j\ll\lvert S\rvert$.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

problem: How to choose which of many candidate research problems to work on next, given limited capacity and an abundance of ideas.
did: Maintained an append-only ideas file and, between projects, skimmed it and picked whichever idea seemed most interesting or important at that moment.
alternatives_named: find something new entirely if nothing looks compelling
passing projects off to lab members
stated_reason: As an independent contributor he can only work on a few things at a time, so each choice means not doing something else; his problem is filtering ideas, not generating them.
quote: When it's time to pick my next project, I skim through the list, and pick whichever I think is most interesting. or exciting. or important. or whatever I'm looking for at the moment.
title: My research idea logfile, 2016-2019

problem: What kinds of tasks should a new LLM benchmark be built from, given that existing benchmarks focus on homework-style problems?
did: Built the benchmark from nearly 100 tests extracted from the author's own real conversation history with LLMs, focused on three types of questions he actually asks.
alternatives_named: homework-style problems typical of existing benchmarks
academic benchmarks of general model capabilities
stated_reason: The questions assigned to students differ from the questions the author wants a model to solve for him.
quote: Existing benchmarks tend to focus on solving typical problems that might be assigned to a student as homework. But the types of questions that are assigned to students are different from the types of questions I want to ask a language model to solve for me.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How should model answers be evaluated so that tests reflect realistic use and can be scored automatically?
did: Built a dataflow DSL that specifies both how to ask the question and how to evaluate the answer, mostly by actually running model-written code in a docker container.
alternatives_named: other evaluation methods supported by the framework
stated_reason: It makes it easy to add new tests that realistically evaluate model capabilities, including the output of code the model writes.
quote: I've implemented a simple dataflow domain specific language to make it easy for me (or anyone else!) to add new tests that realistically evaluate model capabilities. This DSL allows for specifying both how the question should be asked and also how the answer should be evaluated.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How should tasks that are context-specific and impossible to evaluate automatically be handled in the benchmark?
did: Extracted the essence of the task and wrote a corresponding question that can be evaluated.
alternatives_named: evaluating the original context-specific task directly
stated_reason: The original tasks are context-specific and impossible to evaluate automatically.
quote: Or, in cases where the actual task I was asking for is context-specific and impossible to evaluate automatically, I've tried to extract the essence of the task and write a correspodning question.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How strongly should the benchmark be claimed to measure general model capabilities, given its narrow, personal scope?
did: Explicitly stated it is not a good benchmark for general capabilities nor for any specific capability, but a benchmark for the author's own uses.
alternatives_named: presenting it as a general capability benchmark
stated_reason: The model could do many things the author does not ask of it; academic benchmarks exist for that purpose, and the author only cares about getting right answers.
quote: Does this make it a good benchmark for general model capabilities? No. It's possible that the model could do many things I'm just not asking it to do.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: Should the benchmark investigate why a model gets an answer right (memorization vs reasoning) or only whether it does?
did: Chose to measure only whether the answer is right, not the mechanism behind it.
alternatives_named: testing for memorization of previously asked questions
testing for clever reasoning on unseen questions
stated_reason: The author just wants the right answer, so the benchmark is for him rather than for a specific type of capability.
quote: I don't care why the model managed to get the answer right. Did it memorize the answer because someone else asked exactly this same question before? Did it use some clever “reasoning” to solve a question it's never seen before? I don't care---I just want the right answer.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How should prompts be designed when querying models in the benchmark: optimized prompting or plain questions?
did: Used plain, un-engineered prompts, simply typing the question as a normal user would.
alternatives_named: telling the model it is an expert
offering a tip or threatening harm
asking the model to take a deep breath and think step by step
stated_reason: The author is lazy and wants to just type a question and get the right answer, rather than measure optimal-use capability.
quote: I do not want to remind the model it is AN EXPERT IN PYTHON and tell it that I'll give it a $100,000 tip for giving the right answer OR I WILL MURDER A KITTEN but please pause....take a deep breath....and think step by step by step before answering.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How can the emoji-conversion task, which has no ground-truth automatic checker, be scored?
did: Asked the same model to convert its emoji output back into movie titles and scored on that round trip.
quote: To evaluate this task I ask the same model to convert those emoji back into movie titles. Useful? No. Fun? Yes.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How can a model's drawn image output (a .bmp from C code) be verified as correct without human inspection?
did: Passed the generated image to a vision language model, asked what flag it shows, and checked the description for 'United States' or 'USA'.
stated_reason: The framework needs an automated check that the code produced a valid, correct image.
quote: And finally, we verify that the code was correct. To do this, we pass the resulting image to a language model and ask what flag has been drawn.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How to interpret the models' poor performance on tasks involving a newly designed assembly language, which might reflect a hard limit or a threshold of capability.
did: Interpreted the rare successes as indicating the task sits right at the boundary of what is becoming possible with a single model evaluation.
stated_reason: Models mostly fail but succeed in very few cases, even on simple programs like testing primality.
quote: In very few cases they succeed, but it looks like this is right at the boundary of what's just becoming possible to achieve with just a single evaluation of the model.
title: My benchmark for large language models

problem: How to surface evaluation flaws in a defense paper that are evident from the paper itself.
did: Prompted GPT-4 with the best-practices checklist and a screenshot of the paper to flag concerning evaluation results, then manually verified the model's answers.
stated_reason: The impossibility of the claims is sufficiently well understood that the errors need not be described by the author directly.
quote: The impossibility of the claims it makes are sufficiently well understood that, instead of describing the errors ourselves, we prompt GPT-4 with a copy of the checklist in [3], a screenshot of the defense paper [5]
title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre

problem: Whether to trust LLM-generated critiques of the paper's evaluation.
did: Accepted the GPT-4 outputs only after the author personally checked that they were accurate and true.
stated_reason: The model identified the flaws correctly, and the author verified this.
quote: In both of these cases, the language model has correctly identified the flaws in the original paper, and the author of this paper has checked that the model’s response is accurate and true.
title: Cutting through buggy adversarial example defenses: fixing 1 line of code breaks Sabre

problem: How to assess whether the evaluation followed established adversarial robustness standards.
did: Audited the paper item-by-item against the recommended best-practices checklist, e.g. iterative vs single-step attacks, adaptive attacks, ablations.
stated_reason: Sabre deviates from the widely accepted best practices for evaluating adversarial robustness.
